clinical_knowledge.topic: Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes targeted high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal therapy for MSSA, with regimen selection guided by microbiology, renal function, allergy history, and surgical planning, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chills, night sweats, weight loss, and new regurgitant heart murmur with mobile vegetation on echocardiogram

Key HPI features: 53M with history of intravenous drug use presents with 3-week history of high fevers, drenching night sweats, 15-lb weight loss, generalized weakness, and painful reddish spots on the pads of his fingers. Over the past 3 days, developed worsening shortness of breath and ankle swelling.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 110, BP 105/50 (wide pulse pressure), Temp 39.1C. Splinter hemorrhages under nail beds, tender Osler nodes on finger pads, painless Janeway lesions on palms. Auscultation reveals a loud Grade 3/6 blowing diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation at left sternal border. Three sets of blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-sensitive MSSA). Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) reveals a 1.6 cm highly mobile, destructive vegetation attached to the aortic valve leaflets with perforation of the right coronary cusp causing severe acute aortic regurgitation and a 1.2 cm perivalvular aortic root abscess.
Relevant background/PMH: Hepatitis C, active IV heroin/fentanyl injection drug use
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New heart failure symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling) with fever — suggests severe valve destruction needing urgent surgery.
management_principles: Treat MSSA with targeted high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal therapy (e.g., nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin as appropriate); routine synergistic gentamicin is not recommended because nephrotoxicity outweighs unproven benefit

STAT emergency cardiothoracic surgery consultation for urgent operative intervention: aortic root reconstruction and aortic valve replacement with cryopreserved homograft or mechanical/bioprosthetic valve
Surgical indications present: severe acute AR with heart failure, perivalvular root abscess, and large mobile vegetation > 10 mm with embolization risk
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical criteria and peripheral immunological/embolic stigmata of Infective Endocarditis (Modified Duke criteria, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots)

Recognize critical indications for emergent/urgent cardiothoracic surgical valve replacement in endocarditis (refractory heart failure, perivalvular abscess/fistula, persistent bacteremia, large mobile vegetations >10-15 mm)
Compare prosthetic valve selection options (mechanical vs bioprosthetic vs homograft) in active endocarditis and IV drug use
Outline multidisciplinary management combining prolonged targeted IV antimicrobial therapy with complex root debridement/reconstruction

teaching.diagnosis: Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use)
teaching.one_liner: Bacteria introduced through injection drug use seed the aortic valve, destroying the leaflets and causing severe regurgitation, heart failure symptoms, and peripheral immune stigmata like Osler's nodes.
differentials: Sepsis from a skin/soft tissue source
red_flags: New heart failure symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling) with fever — suggests severe valve destruction needing urgent surgery

must_ask.say: Can you tell me about your drug use — what you use and how often you inject?
How long have you had fevers and night sweats?
Have you noticed any tender spots on your fingertips?
Have you had trouble breathing or swelling in your ankles?
How much weight have you lost?
